nature-found-004.title: Ecosystem services: the work nature does for people
nature-found-004.text: New York City had two ways to keep its water clean. It could build a filtration plant, estimated at $6–8 billion plus $300 million a year to run. Or it could restore its Catskill watershed, the land whose streams feed the city's supply, for an estimated $1–1.5 billion. The city chose the land, and the land did the plant's job for a fraction of the cost. That job is an ecosystem service: one of the many benefits people get from ecosystems. Others include pollination of crops, clean air, the breakdown of discarded material and {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} control. These services are vital for human well-being, giving direct and indirect benefits such as clean water, food and a steady climate. The term "environmental services" appeared in a 1970 report, and "ecosystem services" later became the standard term in science. In the early 2000s a United Nations initiative, covered in {{ref:nature-es-001}}, popularised sorting them into four groups: provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural. Economists value these services in dollars using methods such as avoided cost, the cost of replacing a service, travel cost and surveys of what people would pay. A 1997 study put the value of the world's ecosystem services and the natural stocks behind them at US$16–54 trillion per year, averaging US$33 trillion. Some schemes now reward farmers or landowners for managing their land so that it keeps providing a service, an approach explored in {{ref:nature-mkt-136}}.

nature-econ-802.title: Climateflation: when a warming climate raises prices
nature-econ-802.text: Heat, droughts and floods hit farm output, and shoppers feel it at the checkout. Climateflation is inflation driven by {{ref:nature-hist-007}}, through its effects on food production and the networks that deliver goods. Isabel Schnabel of the European Central Bank first used the term. In 2022–2023, climate-driven heat in Europe raised food prices by about 0.7%, adding about 0.3% to overall inflation. The same study found that warming expected by 2035 could raise these effects by 30–50%. A related term, fossilflation, describes inflation caused by fossil fuel prices, which push up transport, food and shipping costs.

nature-found-049.title: Unemployment and inflation as market failures
nature-found-049.text: Some market failures hit the whole economy at once. Unemployment, inflation and an economy thrown out of balance are seen as market failures at that scale. They can follow a financial crash, recession or depression. They show up as an economy producing below its capacity for a long time. The repeated downswings and upswings of an economy are said to call for some government intervention.

nature-found-080.title: Why the best amount of pollution is not zero
nature-found-080.text: Society gets something from pollution: the polluting goods themselves, and lower prices. Otherwise no one would pollute. So the aim is not zero pollution but the socially optimal level, the amount at which society's welfare is greatest. That is where the harm of one more unit equals the benefit of producing it. The free market misses this point, because it ignores pollution's cost to society. The true supply curve sits higher than the market one, and the optimum lies where the curve of marginal social cost meets market demand. At that optimum, output is lower and price higher than in the free market, so the free market outcome is a market failure. A corrective tax proportional to the damage of each extra unit yields the efficient level of pollution reduction. The model is used to compare ways of internalizing the externality, such as import taxes, taxes on the damage like a carbon levy, and cap and trade. Accepting some pollution can raise overall wellbeing, though every increase is still a cost that must be counted.

nature-eco-362.title: Heterotrophs: life that must feed on other life
nature-eco-362.text: Every mushroom is a heterotroph, and so are most animals. A heterotroph is an organism that cannot make its own food. It gets its carbon from other organisms or from their remains. The group includes most animals, all fungi, some bacteria and protists, and many parasitic plants. In the chain of who eats whom, heterotrophs are the consumers. Autotrophs, which make food from sunlight or inorganic chemicals, are the producers. Some heterotrophs eat dead plants, dead animals and feces. Their work keeps the planet's materials moving. Respiration by heterotrophic microbes releases much of the carbon dioxide entering the atmosphere, which plants then take up again. Through mineralization, the release of nutrients locked in dead matter, heterotrophs turn organic nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus into inorganic forms that plants can use. That step is critical to plant survival and to soil fertility.

nature-eco-383.title: Ecological productivity: how fast an ecosystem grows
nature-eco-383.text: Swamps and marshes are listed as producing 2,500 grams of carbon in new biomass on each square meter every year. That figure measures ecological productivity: the rate at which an ecosystem makes new biomass. It is often given in grams per square meter per day. The productivity of plants and other autotrophs is called primary productivity. That of animals and other heterotrophs is secondary productivity. Three things set it: nutrient supply, temperature and water. More is not always better. Nutrients washed in from fertilizer can trigger sudden surges of algae. These raise primary production but leave the ecosystem less stable.

nature-eco-674.title: Ecoregions: mapping nature's distinct communities
nature-eco-674.text: The WWF first set out 867 terrestrial ecoregions in 14 biomes and 8 biogeographic realms. An ecoregion is a large land or water area defined by its environmental resources, with a geographically distinct assemblage of natural communities and species. WWF's definition requires that communities share most of their species and dynamics, share similar environmental conditions, and interact ecologically in ways critical to their long-term persistence. Boundaries rarely form abrupt edges. They are bounded by transition zones between communities and by mosaic habitats, and most ecoregions contain habitats that differ from their assigned biome. Two systems compete. Bailey's algorithmic system gives priority to climate and ecological criteria, while the WWF system, built for biodiversity conservation planning, gives priority to the distribution of species assemblages. A 2017 update with satellite imagery reduced the terrestrial count to 846 and later 844. Marine ecoregions number 232, grouped into 62 provinces and 12 realms, and the freshwater map of 2008 has 426 ecoregions. The Global 200 is WWF's list of priority ecoregions for conservation.

nature-es-086.title: Ecosystem engineers: species that build and reshape habitats
nature-es-086.text: Beavers fell trees and build barriers across streams, and in doing so they change the distribution and abundance of many other organisms. They are the original ecosystem engineer: a species that creates, substantially changes, maintains or destroys a habitat. Such species can strongly affect how many species an area holds and how varied its landscape is. They matter because they modify resources, not because they are eaten. Species covered in {{ref:nature-eco-301}} usually matter through feeding relationships instead. By making habitats more varied, beavers can support species not found elsewhere. Conserving one engineer may therefore protect a whole landscape's diversity. Whales release nutrients at the surface that feed phytoplankton and spread them across oceans, the {{ref:nature-eco-365}}. Introduced species such as kudzu and the zebra mussel often act as engineers. Humans are thought to be the most dramatic engineers of all, through cities, farming, logging, river barriers and mining. Some ecologists see the term as a buzzword, since it may imply intent and every species changes its environment to some degree.

nature-eco-275.title: Surface runoff: when water cannot soak in
nature-eco-275.text: A roof or a parking lot lets no rain soak in at all. Every drop that lands becomes surface runoff, or overland flow. This is water flowing freely over the ground when rain, snowmelt or other water cannot soak into the soil fast enough. On natural ground, runoff starts when the soil is already saturated or when rain arrives faster than infiltration can take it in. Runoff is a major part of the water cycle. It is also the main way water wears soil away, the process covered in {{ref:nature-eco-264}}. Its main environmental harm is what it carries. Running water picks up petroleum, herbicides and fertilizers and delivers them into surface water, groundwater and soil. More runoff also means less water seeping down to refill groundwater, so underground water levels drop and droughts hit harder for people who rely on wells. When a stream cannot carry all the runoff flowing downstream, it floods. The remedies follow from the causes. Limit paved surfaces, control erosion on farms and building sites, build the green networks described in {{ref:nature-nbs-161}}, and control how chemicals are used.

nature-eco-668.title: Where methane comes from
nature-eco-668.text: About 60% of the methane released in 2019 came from human activity: roughly 360 million tons from humans and 230 million tons from natural sources. The 2024 total was estimated at 610 million tons, nearly two-thirds human. The 2021 CCAC and UNEP assessment attributes over 50% of global emissions to people: fossil fuels 35%, waste 20% and agriculture 40%. Biogenic methane is made by methanogens, which live in warm, moist soils and in the digestive tracts of ruminants, which emit it by burping and defecating. Landfills turn anaerobic within about a year of filling, letting methanogens take over. Rice paddies emitted about 30 of 400 million metric tons of anthropogenic methane in 2022. Biomass burning, mostly human-caused, and gas-engine 'methane slip' also release it. Sinks weaken too. Converting forest to farmland adds soil nitrogen, which inhibits methane oxidation and weakens the soil microbes that oxidize methane. Methane mixes through the troposphere in about 1-2 years, and satellite data show over 80% of emission growth in 2010-2019 was tropical and terrestrial. See {{ref:nature-eco-201}} for the gas itself.

nature-eco-279.title: Taming runoff, from medieval fields to city drains
nature-eco-279.text: Since medieval times, farmers have protected their soil by contour farming, plowing across slopes rather than down them. Runoff mitigation combines controls on how land is used, erosion controls, flood control and chemical handling rules to reduce the harm runoff causes. Construction sites use straw bales, silt fences and work scheduled for drier months to slow runoff. Holding ponds buffer peak river flows. In the United States, the federal law described in {{ref:nature-pol-155}} requires urban local governments to run programs for managing storm runoff, under discharge permits.

nature-eco-114.title: Climate change as a threat of extinction
nature-eco-114.text: Today 84% of coral-built reefs could withstand abnormally hot spells at sea. At 1.5 °C of warming, 2022 estimates suggest, only 0.2% could. Climate change can drive species extinct by pushing temperature and weather outside the conditions each evolved to live in, its niche. A species can adapt where it is or move. So far the IUCN links only 20 of 864 recorded species extinctions to climate, usually on weak evidence. Projections are grimmer. A 2011 review of 74 studies found an average projected loss of 11.2% of species by 2100. For insects, a 2018 study looked at three levels of warming: 1.5 °C, 2 °C and 3.2 °C. It estimated that 6%, 18% and about 49% of species, respectively, would lose over half their climatic range. A 2021 estimate that warming like that of the Big Five would bring a similar mass extinction was disputed the next year. At sea, climate already threatens 45% of at-risk species, though fishing and pollution do more damage for now. Prevention means limiting warming and protecting habitat, as in the 30x30 effort.

nature-eco-625.title: Anthropogenic disturbance: when people are the storm
nature-eco-625.text: Logging, dredging, mowing, mining and converting land to ranching or farming all count as anthropogenic disturbance: disturbance to ecosystems caused by human activity. Worldwide, it has spread species suited to disturbed ground, often called weeds. Human disturbance can also sustain. Fires set on purpose by Native Americans maintained fire-dependent ecosystems and helped keep them stable and diverse. Looking ahead, human-caused climate change is considered a major force shaping future ecosystem change, a theme of {{ref:nature-eco-129}}.

nature-eco-442.title: What wetlands do for people, and what they are worth
nature-eco-442.text: One analysis valued the storm protection wetlands provide against hurricanes at US$33,000/hectare/year. That is one of many ecosystem services, the benefits people get from nature, that wetlands supply by storing and cleaning water. The {{ref:nature-es-001}} and the {{ref:nature-gov-051}} list a long roster: flood control, refilling of underground water, storm protection, cleaning of water, biodiversity, products, culture, recreation and a steadier climate. Many wetlands are linked to water stored underground and help refill the porous rock layers that supply much of the world's drinking water. Coastal wetlands protect shores by reducing the speed and height of waves and floodwaters. In highly developed areas, wetlands may be the only habitat left for pollinating insects, birds and mammals. Replacing these services would take enormous sums for treatment plants, river barriers and flood banks, and many could not be replaced at all. According to the Ramsar treaty, intact wetlands are often worth much more to society than the gains people expect from converting them to intensive use.

nature-eco-713.title: The Forest Stewardship Council: certifying wood
nature-eco-713.text: Look for the FSC mark on paper or timber and you are seeing a market-based answer to {{ref:nature-eco-053}}. The Forest Stewardship Council is an international non-profit, multistakeholder organization founded in 1993 that promotes responsible care of forests through timber certification. It runs a global certification system for forests and the goods made from them. Members join one of three chambers: environmental, social and economic. Governments cannot be members and engage only as land owners. FSC does not audit itself. It accredits certification bodies, which then certify forests and companies to its standards. In September 2012 some 165 million hectares in 80 countries were certified, and about 24,000 chain of custody certificates were active in 107 countries. The main competing system is PEFC, criticized for little local or environmental organization influence and lack of transparency.

nature-eco-740.title: Unintended consequences: when actions backfire or surprise
nature-eco-740.text: Actions in complex systems rarely land only where aimed. Unintended consequences are outcomes of a purposeful action that were neither intended nor foreseen. They fall into three types: unexpected benefits, unexpected drawbacks, and perverse results contrary to the intent. Irrigation schemes can supply farm water yet raise the prevalence of waterborne diseases such as schistosomiasis. Cold War no-man's lands became large natural habitats, an unexpected benefit. Adam Smith's invisible hand is another example, in which agents acting in self-interest contribute to overall economic efficiency. Robert K. Merton popularised the term. His 1936 causes include ignorance, errors in analysis and immediate interests overriding long-term ones. Causes also include complexity, incentives that reward the wrong behavior and cognitive biases. The law of unintended consequences warns that intervening in a complex system tends to produce unanticipated, often undesirable outcomes.

nature-eco-463.title: How rivers build their floodplains
nature-eco-463.text: A meandering river eats away the outside of each bend and builds a sandbar, a point bar, on the inside, slowly laying down a level floodplain. Most floodplains are built this way, by rivers depositing sediment both inside their bends and when floods spill over the banks. Water spilling over the banks drops a thin layer of sediment, thickest and coarsest near the channel. Over time this forms low natural ridges along the river's edge. In undisturbed rivers, overbank flow typically happens every one to two years.

nature-val-113.title: Direct damage-cost valuation: counting what pollution breaks
nature-val-113.text: One way to value cleaner air is to add up the damage dirty air does. Direct damage-cost valuation treats an environmental improvement as the reduction in the monetary damage costs of pollution. Types include production damage, such as air pollution lowering corn yields, avoided cost, such as planted roofs avoiding storm sewer spending, and health cost measures. The Cabezas text calls these measures deeply problematic. They often give woefully incomplete estimates, since a cancer victim's medical bills are far below what her family would pay to avoid the illness.

nature-val-110.title: Mild and wild risk: when averages lie
nature-val-110.text: Not all risk behaves alike. Mandelbrot distinguished mild risk, which follows normal or near-normal distributions, from wild risk, which follows distributions with extra-heavy tails. Mild risk obeys the law of large numbers and is relatively predictable. Wild risk, with possibly infinite mean or variance, makes that law ineffective and is hard or impossible to predict. A common error is to assume risk is mild when it is wild. It is a sharper case of {{ref:nature-econ-773}}.

nature-econ-402.title: Price controls: when governments set prices
nature-econ-402.text: Diocletian tried to cap the price of every commodity in the late 3rd century AD, with little success. Price controls are government-enforced limits on the prices that may be charged for goods and services, and they are ancient: the Code of Hammurabi set wages for shipbuilders. There are two main kinds. A ceiling ({{ref:nature-econ-400}}) sets the most that may be charged. A floor ({{ref:nature-econ-405}}) sets the least. Controls on rents and wages are well-known examples. Governments use them to keep goods affordable during shortages, to slow inflation, or to guarantee a minimum income to some providers. Controls are also one of the indirect ways governments subsidize energy. A cap set low tends to backfire. Keeping prices artificially low raises demand beyond what supply can meet, and shortages feed illegal trading at higher prices. During the 1973–74 Arab oil embargo, a US price cap below the market level led to long queues and gas stations running dry. Most Western economists say consumer price controls do not work, though since the 1990s wage floors have won strong support among some economists.

nature-found-018.title: When did the human age begin
nature-found-018.text: Researchers cannot agree on when the human-shaped era of Earth's history began, and the candidates span thousands of years. William Ruddiman argued it began about 8,000 years ago, with farming and settled cultures. Others place it near the start of the Holocene, the present geological epoch, as early peoples cleared forests, hunted giant animals to extinction and spread invading species. Crutzen proposed the Industrial Revolution, and Lovelock proposed the first Newcomen steam engine, in 1712. In 2019 the Anthropocene Working Group proposed the mid-20th century. Then population, industry and farm chemicals surged, and atomic tests left radioactive debris in deposited layers.

nature-nbs-319.title: Dams: holding back rivers
nature-nbs-319.text: There were 62,362 large dams worldwide in 2025, and an estimated 2.8 million human-made dams of any size in 2019. A dam is a structure that impounds water or restricts its flow. Dams provide irrigation, hydropower, water supply, flood management, recreation, inland navigation and fish farming, and many multi-purpose dams serve two or more of these. Human-made dams are classed as embankment, gravity, buttress, arch or composite; natural dams include rockslide, volcanic and beaver-built dams. The costs are real. Dams can alter rivers, habitats, vegetation, biodiversity and microclimates, and often degrade downstream water quality and volume, especially in the dry season. Developers in many countries must prepare an {{ref:nature-pol-132}} so the government can judge a dam's desirability, mitigate impacts and compensate affected people. Reservoirs gradually accumulate sediment, which cuts storage capacity and so the dam's ability to irrigate, generate power or control floods. A dam may be removed if it is a safety hazard, no longer serves its purpose, or to restore fish migration and downstream river health.

nature-nbs-171.title: Sustainable drainage: making pipes behave like soil
nature-nbs-171.text: In urban areas covered mostly by hard surfaces, more than half of the rain becomes runoff. A sustainable drainage system, or SuDS, is a set of practices that make modern drainage work with natural water processes, as part of a wider green infrastructure strategy. SuDS aim to reduce the harm development does to the water cycle, especially runoff and water pollution. They often bypass traditional drains and return rainwater to natural water bodies as soon as possible. Typical parts include grassy drainage channels, porous paving, artificial wetlands, ponds that hold rain, planted roofs, rain-soaking gardens and downspouts cut off from the sewer. Plants and soil remove pollutants by adsorption, where they stick to surfaces, and by filtration and plant uptake. Cost favors them: planting a garden to handle drainage usually costs less than digging tunnels and laying pipes.

nature-nbs-325.title: Detention basins: storing a storm and releasing it slowly
nature-nbs-325.text: A detention basin is an excavated area on or near a waterway that protects against flooding, and sometimes downstream erosion, by temporarily storing water. It lets large flows in and limits outflow through a small low opening sized to downstream culvert capacity, and it can control events such as a 1-in-100-year storm. Basins are usually built with new developments to handle runoff from impervious surfaces like roads, parking lots and rooftops. A basin with no permanent pool is a dry pond. One designed to hold some water permanently is a {{ref:nature-nbs-172}}, which manages quantity but has limited effect on water quality. Real-time control of outflow makes basins significantly better at retaining suspended solids and associated contaminants. Extended detention dry basins lengthen storage time beyond the 6 to 12 hours of basic ponds, allowing more settling of solids and cleaner water. City parks can serve as dual-purpose basins, acting as sports fields or parkland normally and storing stormwater in big storms; Joynton Park in Sydney is an example.

nature-nbs-197.title: Low-impact development: handling rain where it falls
nature-nbs-197.text: Conventional detention ponds in Prince George's County, Maryland, were not cost-effective and missed their water quality goals. So in 1990 the county tried low-impact development, or LID. This North American approach to land planning and engineering manages stormwater runoff as part of green infrastructure. It uses small engineered controls to copy a site's natural water regime, infiltrating, filtering, storing, evaporating and holding runoff near its source. Its five principles: conserve natural areas, minimize the impact on water flows, keep runoff rate and duration, scatter small controls across the site, and prevent pollution. Typical practices include rain gardens, pervious concrete, grassed swales and collecting rainwater. Research found LID rain gardens can hold up to 90% of the water after a major storm and release it over up to two weeks. Developers gain too, since dropping ponds on expensive land lets them build more homes on the same plot. In some municipalities LID is a cost-effective way to reduce spills into rivers, when pipes carrying both rain and sewage overflow.

nature-nbs-322.title: Combined sewers: one pipe for sewage and rain
nature-nbs-322.text: About 860 US communities have combined sewers, serving about 40 million people; the UK has about 22,000 overflows. A combined sewer is a gravity sewer system that carries sewage and urban stormwater runoff together to a treatment plant or disposal site. In rain, sewage is diluted and flows at the treatment site rise. Runoff can pick up sediment, heavy metals, organic compounds, animal waste, and oil and grease. Overflows occur when combined flow exceeds what the treatment plant or sewer can carry. The design has old roots. Early sewers carried street runoff untreated into waterways, and before 19th-century macadam paving, porous surfaces let rain soak away. The link to {{ref:nature-res-261}} is direct, and {{ref:nature-nbs-161}} is one way to reduce the load.

nature-nbs-055.title: Hold the line: keeping the shore where it is
nature-nbs-055.text: Seawalls, groynes, breakwaters set off the shore and revetments make up more than 70% of protected shorelines in Europe. They serve hold the line, a strategy that keeps the shoreline where it is, usually with permanent concrete and rock. Armoring often just moves the problem along the coast, and maintenance costs can eventually force a change of strategy. Holding the line need not mean concrete. Soft options such as beach nourishment and dune stabilization can do it by working with natural processes.

nature-econ-851.title: Progressive tax: rates that rise with income
nature-econ-851.text: Under a progressive tax, the rate climbs as the taxable amount grows, so a taxpayer's average rate stays below the marginal rate. The marginal rate is the one on each extra unit of income. The effective marginal rate is higher still once lost welfare benefits and tax credits are counted. A progressive tax moves the burden toward people with more ability to pay. Its opposite is a {{ref:nature-pol-124}}, such as a sales tax, where the poor pay a larger share of income. It directly reduces {{ref:nature-econ-850}}, especially when it funds transfers and safety nets, though more evasion at higher rates may mute the effect. Brackets that are not indexed to inflation cause bracket creep, an effective tax increase. The effect on growth is disputed. A 2008 OECD report found a weak negative relationship, while the IMF says some advanced economies could raise progressivity without hampering growth. Hayek and Nozick opposed it on principle.

nature-acct-070.title: Environmental indicators: simple numbers for a complex world
nature-acct-070.text: People respond best to clear, simple measures, such as the UV index and the air quality index. That is the logic of the environmental indicator: a simple measure, tracked over time, that tells what is happening in the environment. Indicators are a practical, cheaper way to follow a complex environment than recording every variable. The concentration of chemicals that destroy ozone in the air, for example, indicates the state of the ozone layer in the stratosphere. The OECD's Pressure-State-Response model sorts indicators into three kinds. Pressure indicators include greenhouse gas emissions. State indicators describe the condition of the environment. Response indicators include the number of people served by sewage treatment. Good indicators are judged on scientific credibility, policy relevance and practical data needs. Environmental indicators are a subset of broader indicators of development that also cover social and economic health. Large sets are condensed into indices, headline indicators, traffic-light visuals or dashboards.

nature-acct-119.title: Net domestic product: GDP after the machines wear out
nature-acct-119.text: A country can raise its output by spending more on replacing worn-out machines, and be no better off. Net domestic product (NDP) is gross domestic product minus the depreciation of a country's capital goods. It accounts for capital consumed during the year, such as the wearing out of housing, vehicles and machinery. The amount deducted is often called the capital consumption allowance, the amount needed to replace the depreciated assets. Investment that only replaces worn-out equipment keeps output up but adds nothing to the economy's capacity, so rising GDP from higher replacement spending would not make anyone better off. Some economists therefore see NDP as a better measure of social and economic well-being. A growing gap between GDP and NDP signals increasing obsolescence of capital goods; a narrowing gap means the capital stock is improving. NDP adjusted for the using up of natural resources, called EDP, was proposed as a green alternative but was not formally included in the System of National Accounts.

nature-clim-094.title: The Montreal Protocol: the treaty that worked
nature-clim-094.text: Often called the most successful environmental treaty between nations, the Montreal Protocol protects the ozone layer by phasing out the production of substances that deplete it. It was agreed on 16 September 1987 and entered into force on 1 January 1989. With 198 parties, it was the first universally ratified treaty in UN history. It helped poorer members. Under Article 5 developing countries get extra time to comply, and a financial mechanism under Article 10 helps them pay. The results show. Concentrations of the main CFCs, ozone-destroying chemicals, have levelled off or fallen, and the thinning of the ozone layer over Antarctica is slowly recovering. The treaty also helped mitigation, because HCFCs, which it phases out, are very potent greenhouse gases. It is cited as a precedent that the UN consensus approach to global problems can work.

nature-clim-119.title: Grid storage: saving electricity for later
nature-clim-119.text: Battery costs fell by 90% between 2010 and 2023. Grid storage, technologies connected to the grid that store electricity for later use, has grown with them. It stores surplus power from variable sources such as solar and inflexible ones such as nuclear, then releases it when needed. It is one of three main ways to replace the flexibility fossil fuels gave the grid. As of 2023 pumped hydro was the largest form, at 181 GW, ahead of about 88 GW of batteries. Different jobs need different tools. Lithium-ion batteries suit under 8 hours, flow batteries and compressed air medium durations, and hydrogen and heat seasonal storage. Below 40% variable renewables, storage under 4 hours suffices. At 80% medium-duration storage is needed, and above 90% long-duration storage. Storage can also help restart a grid after a blackout.

nature-clim-237.title: Who should pay for climate change?
nature-clim-237.text: Industrialized countries contributed over two-thirds of the human-made greenhouse gas stock, a stock some call an environmental debt. Who should bear the costs of adaptation and mitigation is fiercely debated, and there is no consensus. One approach charges those who benefit most from the public good of a stable climate. On a utilitarian basis, a case can be made for richer countries carrying most of the mitigation burden. A 2019 study found climate change had already widened the global gap between rich and poor, with poor hot countries growing less. Economics alone cannot settle these questions of equity.

nature-clim-284.title: Biomass: energy and carbon stored in living matter
nature-clim-284.text: Biomass is material produced by the growth of microorganisms, plants or animals. The main types are woody, herbaceous and agricultural, aquatic, animal-derived, microbial and waste-derived. It is a renewable energy source and a chemical feedstock, though its energy content is low relative to coal and petroleum and its oxygen content high. The crops matter. First-generation biofuels and plant-based plastics come from energy-dense crops such as rapeseed, sugarcane or corn, and they raise crop prices and take arable land from food. Second-generation biomass, such as wood chippings, grass or solid waste, is far harder to convert because of its varied mixture of compounds. Research continues because it can reuse waste. Ecologists use the word differently, for the total mass of organisms in an ecosystem, usually expressed as carbon. A 2017 estimate for the whole biosphere is about 550 Gt C, with about 450 Gt C of it in terrestrial plants. Remote sensing such as NDVI is commonly used to estimate biomass over large areas.

nature-eco-130.title: Indirect drivers: the forces behind the bulldozer
nature-eco-130.text: A bulldozer clearing forest is the visible end of a long chain. Indirect drivers are the political, economic and social forces that give rise to the human activities that harm the environment. They include population, growth of the economy, urbanization, technology and climate change. Direct drivers, such as mining, agriculture, urban infrastructure and transport, result from them. Together they shape {{ref:nature-eco-129}}. Consumption beyond what ecosystems can sustain can be measured with the tool described in {{ref:nature-acct-027}}. Impact depends on lifestyle, affluence and pollution as much as on the raw number of people. Cultural values matter too: how a society views nature shapes how hard it works to preserve it. Blaming growing human numbers for environmental problems is controversial. Critics say it can unfairly blame poor people in the Global South.

nature-eco-173.title: Biogeochemical cycles: the planet's recycling loops
nature-eco-173.text: Nothing in an ecosystem is ever truly used up. A biogeochemical cycle is the movement and transformation of chemical elements and compounds between living things, the air and the Earth's crust. Energy and matter behave differently here. Energy flows one way through an ecosystem: it arrives as sunlight and leaves as heat. The matter that makes up living things is instead conserved and recycled. Six elements common in living matter take many chemical forms as they move: carbon, nitrogen, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur. The major cycles include those of carbon, nitrogen and water. In each one, living things change and move a substance, which also passes through stores such as the air, the soil and the oceans. Microorganisms drive much of this cycling. Rocks take part too. The breakdown of rock by weather, erosion, drainage and plate subduction, the slow sinking of one slab of Earth's crust beneath another, all help recycle materials. That mix of life, geology and chemistry is why the cycles are called biogeochemical. Today global warming and other human impacts are changing the speed, intensity and balance of many of them.

nature-eco-245.title: Nutrient pollution: too much of a good thing
nature-eco-245.text: Nitrogen and phosphorus feed crops, but in a lake or a bay they become pollutants. Nutrient pollution is the fouling of water by too many nutrients, usually these two, entering it. It is a main cause of {{ref:nature-eco-216}} in lakes, rivers and coastal waters, where the extra nutrients feed algal growth. Sources include runoff from farms, septic tank waste, feedlots, raw sewage and emissions from burning fuels. Fertilizer that crops do not use is lost from fields and harms air and downstream water. In Europe, agriculture is usually the main source of nitrogen in water, while households and industry often dominate phosphorus. Excess nitrogen brings toxic algal blooms, oxygen-starved water, acidic rain, nitrogen-saturated forests and global warming. The costs are real: dearer water treatment, losses to commercial fishing, fishing for sport and shellfish, and less tourism income. Excess nitrate in drinking water can cause blue baby syndrome. Remedies include vegetated buffer strips, artificial wetlands, better wastewater treatment and permits that make the polluter pay.

nature-eco-256.title: Permafrost: the Arctic's frozen carbon vault
nature-eco-256.text: Frozen soils cover nearly 9% of Earth's land, yet they store between 25 and 50% of the organic carbon in the world's soils. Ground that stays below 0 °C for at least two years in a row is called {{ref:nature-eco-678}}. The Arctic carbon cycle is the part of the global carbon cycle that moves carbon between frozen soils, plants and microbes, the atmosphere and back. The northern circumpolar region alone holds around 1,460–1,600 Pg, or petagrams, of organic carbon in its soils. That is more than double the carbon now in the atmosphere. The carbon is old: radiocarbon dating shows it is often thousands of years old. It got there slowly. Wind and rivers dropped sediment, peat built up, and as the ground surface rose, the buried layers froze into the ground with their carbon locked inside. Early research often overlooked this huge store, but attention has grown enormously since the 2000s. What happens when it thaws is the subject of {{ref:nature-eco-257}}.

nature-eco-262.title: Managing soil carbon: farming as a climate tool
nature-eco-262.text: In the Netherlands, East Anglia and Florida, drained and tilled peat soils have sunk severely as their carbon oxidized. Managing soil carbon means using land in ways that keep or add carbon to soil. It matters because the exchange of carbon between soil and atmosphere is a major part of the global carbon cycle. Humans and farming systems are now the biggest influence on how soil carbon varies. Deforestation, fire, plowing and similar working of the soil, and drainage all cause losses. Adding carbon brings co-benefits: less erosion, higher productivity, cleaner waterways and soil that holds water better. Farming practices that store carbon in soils, covered in {{ref:nature-nbs-226}}, are a land-based way to remove carbon dioxide from the air. Selling that storage is tricky, though. Soil carbon offsets can be hard to verify, because measurements depend on how deep the samples are taken.

nature-eco-281.title: The ecological niche: a species' address and its job
nature-eco-281.text: Every species has a role as well as a place to live. An ecological niche is the particular set of environmental conditions and the role that a species or population occupies in its surroundings. Roswell Hill Johnson coined the word in 1910, and Joseph Grinnell first used it in ecological research in 1917. For Grinnell, a niche was set by a species' habitat and the behaviors that let it persist and reproduce there. In 1927 Charles Elton defined it by an animal's place in the living world, especially its relations to food and enemies. A niche can be described along many axes, such as life history, habitat, feeding position and geographic range. Empty niches get filled. Species brought in from elsewhere may invade the niches of native organisms and outcompete them. Because every species evolved for a certain niche, {{ref:nature-hist-007}}, by shifting temperature and weather, puts species at risk.

nature-eco-288.title: Top-down and bottom-up control of ecosystems
nature-eco-288.text: Is an ecosystem built from below or ruled from above? Both. Trophic dynamics is the transfer of energy and nutrients between organisms. Energy captured by plants passes to herbivores, then carnivores, then top carnivores, and the total shrinks at each higher level. Bottom-up control comes from how much energy plants bring in, top-down control from predators. Correlations in abundance or biomass between consumers and resources are the evidence for bottom-up control, as when herbivore and detritivore biomass rises with primary productivity. Top carnivores keep herbivores in check; without them herbivores could multiply and eat all the plants. If plant populations fall sharply, herbivores decline and then carnivores decline too. An ecosystem need not be one or the other: a marine system may be bottom-up, then come under top-down control during fishing. Predators can dramatically shift which species dominate on land and at sea, and the balance of the two controls is a major research question. Herbivory can also speed the breakdown of litter and nutrient cycling.

nature-eco-297.title: Food webs: the tangled network of who eats whom
nature-eco-297.text: Losing one species can harm a whole chain of others, a knock-on loss described in {{ref:nature-eco-106}}. The reason is the food web, the network of linked feeding sequences in a community that shows who eats whom. Organisms are broadly classed as autotrophs, which make their own food, or heterotrophs, which feed on others. Feeding links fall roughly into four kinds: herbivory (plant-eating), carnivory, scavenging and parasitism. Plants form the base. Top predators sit at the summit, where nothing kills them for food. Energy and matter move differently through a web. Energy moves one way, and eventually all of it is lost as heat. Materials such as nutrients cycle round and round. A feeding sequence usually has at most four or five links, and those in water are often longer than those on land. Charles Elton's 1927 book Animal Ecology made feeding sequences and food cycles central to ecology.

nature-eco-302.title: Primary production: where almost all life's food begins
nature-eco-302.text: Almost every living thing on Earth depends, directly or indirectly, on a single process. Primary production is the making of organic compounds from carbon dioxide in air or water. It happens mainly through {{ref:nature-eco-190}}, the capture of sunlight by plants and algae. The organisms that do it are called primary producers, or autotrophs. They form the base of every feeding chain: mostly plants on land and algae in water. A small share runs on {{ref:nature-eco-696}} instead. It draws energy from chemical reactions of non-living compounds rather than from light. On land, production depends mainly on water and temperature. That is why deserts and polar regions produce so little. Satellites now let scientists add up the whole planet. Their estimate is 104.9 petagrams of carbon a year, with 56.4 made on land and 48.5 in the oceans. The sea, worked by drifting algae, nearly matches the land. Human societies are part of this cycle of production. Yet they influence it far out of proportion to their share of it.

nature-eco-303.title: Gross and net primary production: what plants keep
nature-eco-303.text: A plant spends part of every sugar it makes just staying alive. Gross primary production is all the chemical energy producers capture in a given time. Net primary production is what remains after they use some for their own respiration, the process that releases stored energy. The net share fuels the producers' growth and reproduction, and it is what plant-eaters can eat. Put simply, net equals gross minus the carbon lost to respiration. Gross production is harder to measure, because respiration constantly uses up some of the sugars as they are made. Scaled-up eddy covariance measurements, which track gases flowing between land and air, give a land gross primary production of 123±8 Gt of carbon a year for 1998-2005. Where there is no light, as in caves and hydrothermal vents, microbes that feed on chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide or the gas described in {{ref:nature-eco-727}} are the only producers. A wider measure, {{ref:nature-eco-241}}, also subtracts the respiration of consumers.

nature-eco-327.title: Biomes: the great living regions of Earth
nature-eco-327.text: Under {{ref:nature-hist-007}}, between 22% and 54% of land could end up with climates that match other biomes, and 3.6% with entirely new ones. A biome is a large geographical region with a distinctive climate, vegetation and animal life. Its community forms in response to its physical environment and regional climate. The International Biological Program of 1964–74 popularized the idea. Lines between biomes must be drawn somewhat arbitrarily, because one biome changes gradually into the next. Biomes can shift. The spread of woody plants into open land, which turns grassland into shrubland, is one example of a biome shift.
